limitations: One engine-assisted reviewer used the original Stockfish candidate and played-move comparison lines. Labels were frozen before any nested probe or its result was inspected. Uncertain judgments are explicit.

cases.rationale: Taking first on c5 or dxc5 changes the central pawn structure and the rook files. The exchanges on c4 differ, with no established common tactical payoff.
Black's f-pawn and king try to displace White's king. The leading move orders retain the same blockade and draw.
Rf3+ gains the tempo needed to take h3. White's g-pawn and the rook activity then drive counterplay across the alternatives.
The knight routes alter access to e5 and c4 and change the conditions for the a-pawn advance. The candidate trades on e5 are difficult to separate from ordinary exchanges.
The leading f-pawn advance and lateral rook moves trade king and rook activity for control of pawn targets in a drawable ending.
The bishop choices and knight trades alter pressure against Black's d-pawn and control of the centre. The top scores are close.
The knights can exchange or reroute while the g- and h-pawns change the kingside structure. The alternatives give different exchanges without a clear shared tactical payoff.
White must account for the rook on e4 and use the right capture or checking route. In the resulting queen ending the d-pawn and queen activity persist.
The f-pawn advance creates a concrete sequence with Nf2 and Nh3+ after the captures on g3. Other close choices change the centre and c-file pressure.
The rook pair and extra material give Black several conversions. The f-pawn route enables Nxh3+, while other choices trade queens for activity on different files.
Ne6 gains a tempo on the queen and Ng7+ wins the f5 rook with check. The alternatives allow a materially different capture sequence on f3.
Qh4 introduces Qh1+ and a concrete invasion around White's king. The slower moves give White time for a different defence.
White can prepare the same g-pawn advance with king safety or rook placement. The counterplay is based on Black's f-pawn break and knight manoeuvres.
Bc4+ permits Be6 and a materially different exchange on e6. The leading h-pawn and queen choices maintain pressure with connected attacking pieces and a protected advanced pawn.
Rc8 controls the line before the c5 exchange. Taking first or retreating allows the d-pawn to advance with different forcing threats against the kings.
Queen placement changes which bishop capture and queen checks are available against the king. The f6, d6 and g-pawn structure makes those defensive choices persist.
The bishop and queenside choices change the d-file pressure and both sides' pawn breaks. The played Nf3 changes the exchange on f4, with its tactical relevance uncertain.
The e5 rook can be taken immediately by the queen. The engine's distant alternatives leave it on the board and concede a large concrete advantage.
The stronger minor pieces and active rook hold the initiative. The main fighting chance concerns pawn advance and coordinating the tied pieces.
The bishop can blockade one passed pawn only by conceding other promotion threats. The promotion race and the bishop's diagonal obligations recur across the moves.
Black must keep the king and queen active while White reorganizes around a5. The queen checks change the route but do not demonstrate a separate forced result.
Taking on b5 or preparing first changes how Rxc6 works, including Rxa1 and Rxc8+ in the cross-capture lines. Creation and attack of the c-pawn target persists.
Black's b-pawn gives the queen concrete promotion and check timing. Moving it immediately or after Qa1 changes how White can check and delay promotion.
Neither side can force an entry through the closed pawn chains in the leading lines. Rooks work around the c- and b-files while the knight reroutes.
Black can improve the king before advancing or use the e-file check to bring the rook in. White's c-pawn structure and Black's queenside majority remain important.
White can play Rxh4 to remove the knight immediately or after the c-pawn exchange. Bxh4 and Bxh3 show the material and king-safety costs to calculate.
Qb6+ forces the bishop block, after which Nxe3 and the checking follow-up win material. The weaker knight retreat loses the attack.
The order of Bxc2, Rxb7 and the rook invasion changes the exchanges. The resulting rook activity on the second rank is the common positional concern.
The e-pawn lever and the rook exchange reshape the central files. Be3 instead reroutes the knights and exchanges the kingside bishop.
White can improve the king or keep the rook on an active file. The pawn captures and checks mainly convert the existing rook advantage.
Bxc5 is needed before Black takes the rook on b6. Slow king or knight moves leave a concrete Bxb6 reply.
Qd5+ and f3 can occur in either order while the queen and knight control central squares. The checks alter king placement, with no demonstrated tactical necessity.
Black's rook checks and king routes defend a lost pawn ending. White's more active king and connected future passers determine the plan.
Qxe7 works through Rxf7+ and Bxf7. The resulting passer on c7 is the strategic benefit of the exchange rather than just the first capture.
Bxe5 and Rxc8 must be sequenced to handle Rxc1. The major pieces then contest the open c-file after the central knight is exchanged.
Qd2 avoids the Bxc4 and Rg6 capture sequences. The central king and the f6 knight make several nominal defences fail concretely.
Black's e-pawn advance can promote with check, forcing the rook to give itself up. The passer and bishop coordination dictate the winning plan.
Castling removes the king from the e-file and permits the bishop trade on d6. Bf3 allows Re8+ and further checks, changing rook placement and king safety.
Black must find a safe square for the knight while the white rooks press with checks. The principal continuations have differing counterplay without a clear shared short tactical payoff.
The f-pawn constrains Black's king and rook movements. The kingside and queenside pawn choices change whether Black can activate the rook without conceding the passer.
Nc4 and the b6 break can occur in different orders. They produce the same queenside targets and rook entry, with no clear forced material sequence.
Black chooses the bishop trade or a retreat and different pawn breaks. The Qf5 and Bg6 tempi affect coordination but do not demonstrate a distinct payoff.
The d4 knight, d5 knight and b2 pawn create immediate competing exchanges. The resulting central pawn breaks and b-file use persist after the captures.
The d-pawn advance works because Rd4 drives the bishop back before d2. The alternatives retain a weaker passer and allow different c-file exchanges.
The leading rook and knight choices concede central space but change the d-file and knight outposts. The queen exchange is an available continuation in several lines.
